A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 29 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures supporting comparison. Conflicting settings in v2 are documentation ambiguities rather than missing material.

before.justification: v1 reports original Craftax-classic and Craftax-full experiments, component ablations, and quantitative and qualitative world-model evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds MinAtar experiments, a longer-training configuration, and an annealed policy-update study.

M1.justification: The Dyna, nearest-neighbor tokenizer, and block teacher-forcing framework remains. Appendix F introduces a MinAtar adaptation using layer normalization, Swish, shared actor-critic weights, and revised reward, termination, and entropy loss weights; Section 4.3 also introduces an annealed imaginary-policy update variant. These are localized extensions of the existing method.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates Craftax-classic and Craftax-full. v2 retains both and adds four MinAtar tasks: Asterix, Breakout, Freeway, and SpaceInvaders, using binary 10-by-10 object-channel observations. This substantially broadens evaluated task and input coverage, although all environments remain grid based.

E2.justification: Craftax-full Table 2 adds the MBRL comparator from Cohen et al. (2025), reporting 6.59% reward. The Craftax-classic comparator set remains unchanged. MinAtar extends comparisons among the existing MFRL and M1–M5 approaches.

E3.justification: The new slow Craftax-classic configuration increases world-model updates from 500 to 4,000. MinAtar adds 2,000 world-model and imaginary-policy updates, evaluation every 50,000 steps on 32 environments for 2,000 steps each, and MFRL-normalized aggregation. Existing reported settings also change, including the TD-loss coefficient from 2 to 1 and transformer configuration from eight layers/three heads to three layers/eight heads; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and new Appendix C test whether gradually increasing imaginary-policy updates removes the performance drop when imagination training begins. v2 also extends cumulative component comparisons to MinAtar. The existing patch-size, quantization, warmup, component-removal, RNN, and rollout analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions specify means and standard errors over ten seeds. v2 continues this reporting practice for additional results, explicitly using ten seeds for MinAtar. No increased repeat count or new statistical estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains 67.42% reward and 27.91% score as the fast variant and adds 69.66% and 31.77% under longer training. Craftax-full Table 2 replaces 5.44%/1.53% with a slow configuration reporting 7.20%/2.31%; its settings are not sufficiently consistent for a same-setting comparison. v2 also adds MinAtar results, the annealing reward of 65.71±1.11%, and revised tokenizer-reconstruction curves in Figure 12, formerly Figure 8.

T1.justification: Algorithms 3 and 5 revise minibatch-boundary arithmetic to use the number of environments divided by the number of minibatches, replacing multiples of the minibatch count. This changes the mathematical batch specification. The main probability factorizations, loss formulae, and complexity arguments remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The conclusion newly claims transfer to MinAtar and changes the remaining generalization goal from beyond Craftax to beyond grid-world environments. The headline performance figures increase, while the central contributions and claims of state-of-the-art Craftax performance and superhuman reward remain.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the low-dimensional-memory explanation as intuition and removes the claim that inaccurate imagined trajectories pollute the replay buffer. Appendix F adds discussion of costly terminal-state mistakes and action collapse, explaining the associated loss adjustments. The existing patch-size and appearance-variation limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds a detailed MinAtar adaptation recipe, and Table 1 reports the slow variant's 2,749-minute training time. Existing documentation revises instance normalization to batch normalization, architecture and loss settings, and pseudocode. However, Appendix E states both 48 and 16 Craftax-full environments, while its buffer-size statement conflicts with Table 6. Code-access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 3.6 newly relates BTF to Retentive Environment Models, acknowledging shared parallel prediction while distinguishing transformer applicability from retentive networks. v2 adds citations for this comparison, M3, MinAtar, and implementation components, and removes the Machado-supported Atari memorization argument. The broader research positioning remains.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted wording and notation edits, distinguishes fast and slow variants, and adds Section 4.6, Appendices C and F, and acknowledgments. Earlier Appendices C and D become D and E. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds MinAtar learning curves, an aggregate plot and tabular results display in Figures 7–9, the annealing plot in Figure 11, and adaptation Tables 7–8. Existing performance plots and Tables 1–2 incorporate the slow configuration, while Table 6 gains a buffer-size row. This substantially expands the visual presentation beyond simple renumbering.

improvement.justification: The MinAtar comparisons and annealing study strengthen the evidence beyond v1's Craftax-focused evaluation, and Appendix F documents the required adaptations. These provide a useful but bounded improvement: applicability remains confined to grid environments, the higher headline result requires substantially more computation, and contradictory Craftax-full settings in Appendix E and Table 6 weaken reproducibility.
